chapter: Boyhood and the West End camps
title: How the camp picnics were paid for with advertising cards
summary: Organizers sold ad cards to businesses so band, food and liquor were covered before the picnic.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: All day, all day. From nine to morning, six at night. What paid for all that, Dick, they used to put out an ad card and then take it around to the business people and get a five or ten dollar ad. Well, before they threw the picnic, everything was paid for. The band, the eats, the liquor, whatever they had was paid for. And what would they do with these cards? Well, they'd just put them around town as advertisements, see.
They'd have the advertisement for the picnic and for the...
That's right. The place of business would have a spot, whatever they bought. Two dollars spot, five dollars spot, ten dollars spot. And then they'd place them around town as advertisements.
Well, that was worth it to them, I guess, too. It worked out fine.

It worked out fine for everybody. It worked out fine for the people giving the picnic. They'd pay for everything. And what they got took in, these dollars they took in, was all great. They had card paid for the paying and the eats. And whatever they took in in the admissions was great. And they had them, oh man, they had three or four of them on a Sunday. Mellon Boyd was a hot spot for all their paintings.
